clue.text: Free water

blocks.note: first meaning: to release someone, as in breaking a prisoner out of jail
second meaning: a natural source where water rises from the ground

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words sound like an offer of free drinking water, but each is a separate meaning of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: To spring a prisoner is to set them loose, and a spring is a place where groundwater wells up to the surface.

clue.text: A state of pure chaos

indicators.note: chaos is total disorder, so the letters beside it are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A description of some country or condition sunk in utter turmoil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a condition, as in a state of chaos, but here it means a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Peru is a sovereign South American country, and a country is a state in the political sense.

clue.text: Changed round when batting team has been dismissed

blocks.note: in cricket the batting side is said to be in
a side is a sporting team
a dismissed batsman is out

explanation.surface: A cricket scene: the innings ends and the teams swap over.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture makes 'changed round' sound like teams swapping ends after an innings, but it describes something reversed, like a garment turned so its lining shows.
explanation.definitionFit: Something turned inside out has been reversed so its inner surface faces outward, which is changed round.

clue.text: Yet his talk is far from uplifting!

definitions.text: Yet his talk is far from uplifting!

blocks.clueFragment: Yet his talk is far from uplifting!
blocks.note: surface reading: a speaker whose conversation is dull and depressing
setter's reading: the bag of gas that lifts a balloon or airship is literally uplifting, yet this windbag's chatter is not

explanation.walkthrough: 'Yet' contrasts the two senses: the balloon part gives lift, while the person so named talks endlessly and tediously.
explanation.definitionFit: A gasbag is slang for someone who talks too much and to little purpose, and also the gas container of a balloon.

clue.text: Waste of a key public service

blocks.note: F is one of the musical keys
a utility is a public service such as gas, water or electricity supply

explanation.surface: A complaint that a public service such as a water company is wasteful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' suggests a lock, but here it is a musical key named by a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Futility is pointlessness, effort spent for no result, which is a waste of time and labour.

clue.text: How one may get down to make money dishonestly?

definitions.text: How one may get down to make money dishonestly?

blocks.note: surface reading: how a person might come to be lowered or brought low
setter's reading: down is soft feathers, which a bird gathers to line its home
the idiom for profiting selfishly or corruptly, often from a position of trust

explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' reads as a direction, but it is the soft plumage a bird uses to line its nest, giving the idiom for enriching oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: To feather one's nest is an idiom for making money for yourself, especially improperly while in a position of trust.

clue.text: Mythical king who never quite got what he wanted

definitions.text: Mythical king who never quite got what he wanted

blocks.note: surface reading: a legendary ruler from Greek myth

blocks.clueFragment: never quite got what he wanted
blocks.note: setter's reading: he was punished by standing in water that receded and under fruit that rose whenever he reached for them

explanation.walkthrough: This is close to a plain definition; the gentle understatement 'never quite' is the cryptic touch, since his punishment kept everything just out of reach.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this king was condemned to stand beside water and fruit forever out of reach, which gives English the verb tantalise.

clue.text: Runner defeated in close race

indicators.note: in says the wanted letters sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the run of letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: An athlete who just missed out in a tight finish.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a single sentence about a race, but 'in' is the signal that the answer is buried in the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A runner who is beaten in a race is a loser, the one who did not win.

clue.text: Pitcher on the table?

blocks.note: surface reading: a jug for pouring, set on the table
setter's reading: a device struck on a table top to sound a true musical pitch, and table cutlery shares its name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitcher' suggests a water jug; it means something that gives a pitch, which a musician taps on a hard surface such as a table.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuning fork is a two-pronged steel instrument that sounds a fixed note when struck, used to set the pitch.

clue.text: Man rises above it

blocks.note: surface reading: a person rising above a problem, being superior to it
setter's reading: the Isle of Man, which stands up out of the sea between Britain and Ireland

explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like any person; it is the Isle of Man, a self-governing island lying between Great Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man sits in the stretch of sea separating Great Britain from Ireland, so it rises out of those waters.

clue.text: Snooping, a small number make notes

blocks.note: No. is the short form of number
to sing is to produce musical notes

explanation.surface: A busybody takes a few notes while spying on others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make notes' suggests jotting things down, which fits snooping, but here the notes are musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosing around means prying or poking into other people's affairs, which is snooping.

clue.text: An order for despatch

blocks.note: surface reading: a commercial order for goods to be sent out
setter's reading: to despatch someone is to kill them, and the order is an authority for an execution

explanation.walkthrough: 'Despatch' suggests posting a parcel; it is also the old sense of putting to death.
explanation.definitionFit: A death warrant is the official document authorising someone's execution, an order for them to be put to death.

clue.text: A meal's been cooked for sailors

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these words are mixed into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The ship's galley has prepared dinner for the crew.
explanation.definitionFit: Able seamen are ratings in the navy or merchant navy, so they are sailors.

clue.text: Destructive bore in Spanish river

indicators.note: something destructive breaks things apart, so the word is smashed and its letters reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A damaging tidal wave surging up a river in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: A bore is a tidal wave that surges up a river, so it fits the surface neatly but is only the letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ebro is one of the longest rivers in Spain, flowing to the Mediterranean in the northeast.

clue.text: Complete cancellation of a golf match?

blocks.note: first meaning: to finish something off neatly
second meaning, read whimsically: a round of golf that is called off

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is a playful split of the phrase: a round being off. The question mark flags that liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: To round off is to bring something to a satisfying finish, while a golf round that is off has been cancelled.

clue.text: Such trees are barely recognisable in winter

definitions.text: Such trees are barely recognisable in winter

blocks.note: surface reading: hard to make out or identify
setter's reading: these trees are recognised in winter because they stand bare, having shed their leaves

explanation.walkthrough: 'Barely' seems to mean 'hardly', but it means 'by being bare': such trees drop all their leaves each autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: Deciduous trees shed their foliage every autumn and stand leafless through the cold months, unlike evergreens.

clue.text: Shaken and upset

blocks.note: first meaning: physically stirred or churned, as a liquid in a machine
second meaning: anxious and disturbed in mind

explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like one description of a distressed person, but one is the physical sense and the other the emotional.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitated describes a liquid that has been stirred vigorously and also a person who is nervous or troubled.

clue.text: Confine Brown without leave to military HQ

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one word goes around the other

blocks.note: to pen is to shut in, as with livestock
tan is a light brown colour
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: Someone named Brown is confined to base at headquarters for being absent without leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without leave' reads as the military AWOL, fitting the scene, but the go-word sits inside the colour, which then follows the pen. The Pentagon is the US defence headquarters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pentagon, in Virginia, houses the US Department of Defense, making it the country's chief military headquarters.

clue.text: Grain of discomfort

blocks.note: first meaning: cereal crops such as wheat or maize
second meaning: a painful patch of hard skin on the foot

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grain of discomfort' sounds like a small amount of unease; the two nouns are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Corn is cereal grain, and a corn is a small, sore thickening of skin on a toe, a source of discomfort.

clue.text: Does it secure tile to shingle?

definitions.text: Does it secure tile to shingle?

blocks.note: surface reading: a roofer fixing a roof tile onto wooden shingles
setter's reading: tile is old British slang for a hat, and a shingle is a short, close-cut women's hairstyle

explanation.walkthrough: The roofing words are both disguises: a tile is a hat and a shingle is a bobbed haircut of the 1920s, so the device pins hat to hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatpin is a long decorative pin pushed through a woman's hat and her hair to keep the hat in place.

clue.text: Abandon Britain, say, to live in isolation here?

definitions.note: a place described by what happens there, rather than a noun synonym

blocks.note: to desert is to abandon
Britain is an example of an island, which 'say' signals

explanation.surface: Someone leaving Britain behind to live a solitary life somewhere remote.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description ending in 'here', with the question mark admitting it is a whimsical one.
explanation.definitionFit: A desert island is an uninhabited isle, the classic place where a castaway lives alone, cut off from society.

clue.text: Dis duck - or dat?

indicators.note: dis for 'this' sets up a comic accent that drops the th sound, so the clue is meant to be heard in that voice

blocks.note: 'this or that' in the accent becomes 'dis or dat', so the word before the pair, 'either', is said with a d

explanation.surface: A comic query about which of two ducks is meant, in a broad accent.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as 'either this duck or that?' spoken in an accent turning th into d, so either comes out as the name of a duck.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large sea duck of northern coasts, prized for the soft down used in eiderdowns.

clue.text: Guide to the first card

blocks.note: first meaning: to show the way, conduct
second meaning: in card games, the card played first in a trick

explanation.walkthrough: 'Guide to' sounds like a handbook on cards, but 'to' only joins two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To lead is to guide others, and in card games the lead is the opening card played to a trick.

clue.text: Wrongly admits to being at the centre of things

indicators.note: wrongly means incorrectly arranged, so the letters must be put in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone falsely confesses to having been at the heart of events.
explanation.definitionFit: Amidst is a preposition meaning in the middle of, surrounded by, so it places something centrally among others.

clue.text: One has a job to get money from one

definitions.text: One has a job to get money from one

blocks.clueFragment: One has a job to get money from one
blocks.note: surface reading: someone who struggles hard to extract cash from another person
setter's reading: whoever holds a position draws wages from the person or firm that hires them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Has a job to' suggests difficulty, as in 'has a job getting money'; read literally, holding a job is how you get paid by this person.
explanation.definitionFit: An employer is the person or company that hires staff and pays their wages.

clue.text: Odd doctrine obtains goods without paying

definitions.note: describes buying this way; the answer itself is an adverbial phrase

indicators.note: odd means strange or irregular, so the word is to be put in an unusual order

blocks.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A strange creed that lets its followers take things without paying.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying on credit means taking goods now and settling the bill later, so nothing is paid at the time.

clue.text: The game's finished without a team

blocks.note: no means having none, so without
a side is a sporting team

explanation.surface: A match called off because one team failed to turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby the referee calls 'no side' to end a match; it is the rugby equivalent of the final whistle.
explanation.definitionFit: No side is the traditional rugby term announced when time is up and play stops, meaning the match is over.
